cards.title: 4.1.1 Work Done by a Constant Force
body: A constant force F (constant in magnitude and direction) acting on a body of mass m.
The force makes an angle θ with the displacement s, where θ is the angle between the directions of the force and the displacement.
The work done by the constant force is defined to be the product of the magnitude of the displacement and the component of the force in the direction of the displacement.
A weightlifter holding a load steadily on his shoulder for certain time performs no work on the load during that time.

cards.title: 4.1.2 Work done by a Linearly Varying Force
body: A force whose magnitude increases (or decreases) linearly over time is said to be linearly varying force.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: Which of the following physical quantities is the correct SI unit of work?

steps.text: **Given:** Physical unit of work.
**Formula:** In the SI system, work is measured in Joules ($$\text{J}$$), which is equivalent to Newton-meters ($$\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$$).
**Substitution:** Comparing options: Newton is for force, Watt is for power, Erg is a non-SI CGS unit of work, and Joule is the correct SI unit.
**Final Result:** The correct option is **C. Joule**.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: A person carries a heavy suitcase of mass $$15.0\text{ kg}$$ and walks horizontally a distance of $$20.0\text{ m}$$ at a constant speed. The work done by the lifting force on the suitcase is:

steps.text: **Given:** Mass $$m = 15.0\text{ kg}$$, distance $$s = 20.0\text{ m}$$, vertical lifting force, horizontal motion.
**Formula:** $$W = Fs \cos\theta$$
**Substitution:** The upward lifting force is perpendicular to the horizontal displacement.
Thus, the angle $$\theta = 90^\circ$$, and since $$\cos 90^\circ = 0$$, we get $$W = Fs(0) = 0$$.
**Final Result:** The work done by the lifting force is **Zero**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A metal block of mass $$15.0\text{ kg}$$ is moving with a constant velocity of $$4.0\text{ m/s}$$. What is the kinetic energy possessed by the block?
cards.why:
**Given:** Mass $$m = 15.0\text{ kg}$$, velocity $$v = 4.0\text{ m/s}$$.

**Formula:** $$KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$$

**Substitution:** $$KE = \frac{1}{2}(15.0\text{ kg})(4.0\text{ m/s})^2 = 0.5(15.0)(16.0) = 120.0\text{ J}$$.

**Final Result:** The kinetic energy is **$$120.0\text{ J}$$**.

body: W=F s cosθ KE=½mv² PE=mgh P=W/t=Fv
Work–energy: net work = ΔKE. Mechanical energy conserved if no heat/friction (school ideal).

cards.title: 4.2.1 Kinetic Energy
body: A heavy ball, thick bed of wet sand, metre stick What to do • Take the heavy ball.
Drop it on a thick bed of wet sand. • First drop the ball on the sand bed from a height of about 10 cm.
A moving body can perform work on another body that it collides with or strikes.
For example, a moving hammer performs work on the nail it strikes.

cards.title: 4.2.2 Work-Energy Theorem
body: When a constant force, F acts on the body, for a certain time, it is displaced through a distance s.
The work done by the force causes, a change in the velocity of the body from u to v.
The work done on a body is related to the change in its kinetic energy.
The work-energy theorem states that the work done on a body is equal to the change in the kinetic energy.

cards.title: 4.2.3 Potential Energy
body: The word potential means possibility or the ability to act.
Potential energy is stored energy that can either perform work or be converted to kinetic energy.
The stretched bow-string possesses energy.
When it is released, the arrow flies off at speed.

cards.title: 4.2.4 Mechanical Energy
body: The sum of the kinetic energy and potential energy is called the **total mechanical energy**, or simply mechanical energy.
Energy can be transferred from one place to another or it can be stored.
For example, a book resting on a shelf has potential energy.
At the same time, it gains kinetic energy, since its velocity is increasing.

cards.title: 4.2.5 Conservation of Total Energy
body: **A conservation law** is a law of physics which refers to a quantity that does not change with time is a conservation law.
Conservation laws are often considered to be the most fundamental laws of physics.
The law of conservation of energy states that “Energy can it be created nor destroyed”.
No violation of this principle has ever been found.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The Work-Energy Theorem states that the net work done on an object by a resultant force is always equal to the change in its:
cards.why:
**Given:** Basic physical theorem statement.

**Formula:** $$W_{net} = \Delta KE$$

**Substitution:** According to the work-energy theorem, the total work done by all forces equals the change in kinetic energy of the object.

**Final Result:** The correct option is **C. Kinetic energy**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following is the standard SI unit of power?
cards.why:
**Given:** Unit of power.

**Formula:** Power is work divided by time. In SI, the unit is Joules per second ($$\text{J/s}$$), which is defined as the Watt ($$\text{W}$$).

**Substitution:** Comparing options: Joule is for energy, Horsepower is a British unit of power, Watt-second is a unit of energy, and Watt is the SI unit of power.

**Final Result:** The correct SI unit of power is **C. Watt**.

cards.title: 4.3 Power
body: The same amount of work will have been done in each case but there is something different – the rate at which work is done.
**The average power P** is the work done divided by the time it takes to do the work, or work per unit time.
A common unit of electrical power is the kilowatt (kW), and 1 kW = 1000 W.
In applying a force of 1 N to raise a mass of 1 kg a distance of 1 m, the amount of work done is 1 J.
For example, a 100 W bulb, which 100 joules of electrical energy each second (100 W = 100 J/s).

cards.title: Work needs a push along a path.
body: 90° force does zero work. Power is how fast you work. Energy is the stored ability to work.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Mechanical efficiency ($$\eta$$) is mathematically defined as the ratio of:

options.A: A. Power input to power output
options.B: B. Useful work output to total energy input
options.C: C. Total energy input to useful work output
options.D: D. Friction force to normal force

cards.why:
**Given:** Definition of mechanical efficiency.

**Formula:** $$\eta = \frac{\text{Useful work output}}{\text{Total energy input}} \times 100\% = \frac{W_{out}}{E_{in}} \times 100\%$$

**Substitution:** Comparing definition with choices, option B represents useful work output to total energy input.

**Final Result:** The correct option is **B. Useful work output to total energy input**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: On a graph of force versus displacement, the area under the plotted curve represents the:

options.C: C. Work done by the force

cards.why:
**Given:** Force-displacement graph.

**Formula:** $$\text{Area} = y \times x = F \times s$$

**Substitution:** Since the product of force and displacement is work, the area under the curve represents the work done by the force.

**Final Result:** The correct option is **C. Work done by the force**.

cards.answer: C. Work done by the force

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A motor lifts a 50 kg load through 10 m in 20 s. What is its useful power output? ($g = 10$ m/s²)
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Work done = $mgh = 50 \times 10 \times 10 = 5000$ J.

**Step 2:** Power = work ÷ time.

**Step 3:** $P = 5000 / 20 = 250$ W.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

glossary.meaning: Work done is a scalar quantity and its SI unit is the joule (J).
Potential energy is defined as the energy possessed by a body due to its position or state or configuration (composition).
Gravitational potential energy is the potential energy of the body–Earth system.
Elastic potential energy is a scalar quantity.
Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by a body due to its motion.
Power is defined as the time rate of performing work.

Work done is a scalar quantity and its SI unit is the joule (J).
No work is done if, the displacement of the body is zero, or the force acting is zero or the force and the displacement are mutually perpendicular.
The work done by the frictional force is negative.
The area below the force and displacement graph represents the work done by the force.
Activities like writing, singing, playing, jumping, running, and cycling require energy.
In general, the activities that are tiring require energy.
Machines also require energy to perform work. Therefore, energy is required to perform work.
We cannot imagine our lives without energy.
The sun is the main source of natural energy.
